# Program version and list of changes
Version: 1.0.14



# Welcome message
Ichnaea-MST is a set of R scripts designed for training and classification using the H2O machine learning framework, specifically H2O AutoML. This tool automates model creation and tuning, allowing users to train multiple models and select the best one without manual intervention. It also handles data preprocessing, such as scaling, centering, and encoding categorical variables. Developed for novice users, Ichnaea-MST aims to help the microbiology community explore machine learning in Microbial Source Tracking (MST) scenarios. Users can access the software locally via an R Notebook or remotely through a web-based GUI under a Shiny application.

```{r}
# Show a dialogue box with a welcome message 
svDialogs::dlg_message('Welcome to the "Ichnaea-MST training and classification module." This module trains a self-learning model using H2O AutoML, which can be saved for future use. The trained model can classify samples and reduce MST parameters, and it includes a function to simulate sample decay. Check the help tutorials before using the module. If you have a trained model, use the "Ichnaea-MST UPLOAD AND CLASSIFICATION MODULE." To start, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res
```



# Some libraries and functions that are used to open and save data in various formats, launch spreadsheet applications and determine divergence and detect values under LOD.
This section includes the functions for data file manipulation, the DataExplorer library for creating descriptive statistics, the function to launch a spreadsheet application (Excel o LibreOffice Calc) and a function to determine the Jensen-Shannon divergence between the training sets and the classification sets.

The Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) is a statistical measure that quantifies the similarity between two probability distribution, which is characterised by its symmetry and the fact that it always yields a finite value between 0 and 1. A Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) value of 0.0 indicates that the distributions are identical, meaning there is no difference between the datasets. It is evident from the data that values between 0.0 and 0.2 indicate highly similar distributions, thus suggesting that the model is likely to demonstrate effective generalisation. When the JSD falls between 0.2 and 0.4, it reflects moderate differences, which may introduce slight bias in classification. A range of 0.4 to 0.6 indicates significant disparities, suggesting that the model may be influenced by distributional shifts. Finally, a JSD value greater than 0.6 indicates markedly divergent distributions, suggesting that the model may encounter difficulties with generalisation due to substantial disparities between the training and classification data. 

This renders JSD particularly advantageous in machine learning and data analysis for the detection of distribution shifts, such as when comparing training and prediction datasets to evaluate potential model bias or generalisation issues.


```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(readr)       # To read and write CSV files

library(writexl)     # To write Excel files (xlsx)

# Function to import data from various file formats
import_data <- function(file_path) {
  # Get the file extension
  file_extension <- tools::file_ext(file_path)
  
  # Select the appropriate reading method based on the file extension
  switch(file_extension, 
         csv = read_csv(file_path),     # Read CSV files
         xlsx = read_excel(file_path),  # Read Excel files
         txt = fread(file_path),        # Read text files
         ods = read_ods(file_path),     # Read ODS files
         dta = read_dta(file_path),     # Read Stata files
         sav = read_sav(file_path),     # Read SPSS files
         stop('Unsupported file format') # Throw an error if the format is unsupported
  )
}

# Function to save data to various file formats
save_data <- function(data, file_path) {
  # Get the file extension
  file_extension <- tools::file_ext(file_path)
  
  # Select the appropriate writing method based on the file extension
  switch(file_extension, 
         csv = fwrite(data, file_path),              # Write CSV files
         xlsx = write_xlsx(data, file_path),         # Write Excel files
         txt = fwrite(data, file_path, sep = "\t"),  # Write text files with tab delimiters
         ods = write_ods(data, file_path),           # Write ODS files
         dta = write_dta(data, file_path),           # Write Stata files
         sav = write_sav(data, file_path),           # Write SPSS files
         stop("Unsupported file format")             # Throw an error if the format is unsupported
  )
}

# Try to launch the default application to open the spreadsheet containing data
launch_spreadsheet <- function() {
  # File selection dialog
  filename <- svDialogs::dlg_open(
    title = "Select the spreadsheet file to open",
    filters = svDialogs::dlg_filters[c('All'), ]
  )$res

  if (is.null(filename) || filename == "") {
    cat("No file selected. Operation cancelled.\n")
    return(invisible())
  }

  # Normalize path
  filename <- normalizePath(filename, winslash = "\\", mustWork = FALSE)

  # Warn if file is in OneDrive
  if (grepl("OneDrive", filename, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
    warning("⚠️ The file is located in a OneDrive folder. This may cause issues When is opened.")
  }

  # Remove LibreOffice lock file if it exists
  lock_file <- file.path(dirname(filename), paste0(".~lock.", basename(filename), "#"))
  if (file.exists(lock_file)) {
    message("Removing existing lock file...")
    file.remove(lock_file)
  }

  # Detect OS and define LibreOffice Calc path
  os_type <- Sys.info()[["sysname"]]
  libreoffice_cmd <- NULL

  if (os_type == "Windows") {
    possible_paths <- c(
      "C:\\Program Files\\LibreOffice\\program\\scalc.exe",
      "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\LibreOffice\\program\\scalc.exe"
    )
    for (path in possible_paths) {
      if (file.exists(path)) {
        libreoffice_cmd <- path
        break
      }
    }

    if (!is.null(libreoffice_cmd)) {
      cmd <- paste("start", shQuote(libreoffice_cmd), shQuote(filename))
      shell(cmd, wait = TRUE)
      cat("✅ LLibreOffice Calc or Excel is launched successfully.\n")
    } else {
      warning("🛑 LibreOffice Calc not found in standard locations.")
    }

  } else if (os_type == "Linux") {
    Sys.setenv(LD_LIBRARY_PATH = "/usr/lib/libreoffice/program")
    libreoffice_cmd <- "libreoffice"
    result <- system2(command = libreoffice_cmd, args = c("--calc", shQuote(filename)), wait = FALSE)
    if (result == 0) {
      cat("✅ LLibreOffice Calc or Excel is launched successfully.\n")
    } else {
      warning("⚠️ Failed to launch LibreOffice Calc.")
    }

  } else if (os_type == "Darwin") {  # macOS
    libreoffice_cmd <- "/Applications/LibreOffice.app/Contents/MacOS/soffice"
    result <- system2(command = libreoffice_cmd, args = c("--calc", shQuote(filename)), wait = FALSE)
    if (result == 0) {
      cat("✅ LLibreOffice Calc or Excel is launched successfully.\n")
    } else {
      warning("⚠️ Failed to launch LibreOffice Calc.")
    }

  } else {
    warning("🛑 Unsupported operating system.")
  }

  return(invisible())
}

# launch_spreadsheet() <- to a window to select the file & to open it in Calc

# Divergence function (JSD+TVD)
# Load required library
library(philentropy)

# Normalize a vector to a probability distribution
normalize <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  freq <- table(x)
  prob <- freq / sum(freq)
  return(prob)
}

# Jensen-Shannon Divergence
calculate_jsd <- function(p, q) {
  all_vals <- union(names(p), names(q))
  p_full <- rep(0, length(all_vals))
  q_full <- rep(0, length(all_vals))
  names(p_full) <- all_vals
  names(q_full) <- all_vals
  p_full[names(p)] <- p
  q_full[names(q)] <- q
  mat <- rbind(p_full, q_full)
  tryCatch({
    as.numeric(distance(mat, method = "jensen-shannon"))
  }, error = function(e) NA)
}

# Total Variation Distance
calculate_tv <- function(p, q) {
  all_vals <- union(names(p), names(q))
  p_full <- rep(0, length(all_vals))
  q_full <- rep(0, length(all_vals))
  names(p_full) <- all_vals
  names(q_full) <- all_vals
  p_full[names(p)] <- p
  q_full[names(q)] <- q
  sum(abs(p_full - q_full)) / 2
}

# Interpretation functions
interpret_jsd <- function(jsd) {
  if (is.na(jsd)) "Not computable"
  else if (jsd == 0) "Identical"
  else if (jsd <= 0.2) "Very similar"
  else if (jsd <= 0.4) "Moderate difference"
  else if (jsd <= 0.6) "Notable difference"
  else "Very different"
}

interpret_tv <- function(tv) {
  if (is.na(tv)) "Not computable"
  else if (tv < 0.1) "Very similar"
  else if (tv < 0.3) "Moderate difference"
  else if (tv < 0.5) "Notable difference"
  else "Very different"
}

# Overall interpretation based on average score
overall_interpretation <- function(jsd_int, tv_int) {
  interpretations <- c(jsd_int, tv_int)
  score_map <- c(
    "Identical" = 0,
    "Very similar" = 1,
    "Moderate difference" = 2,
    "Notable difference" = 3,
    "Very different" = 4,
    "Not computable" = NA
  )
  scores <- score_map[interpretations]
  avg_score <- mean(as.numeric(scores), na.rm = TRUE)
  
  if (is.na(avg_score)) {
    return("Not computable")
  } else if (avg_score <= 1) {
    return("Very similar")
  } else if (avg_score <= 2) {
    return("Moderate difference")
  } else if (avg_score <= 3) {
    return("Notable difference")
  } else {
    return("Very different")
  }
}

# Main function to compare all predictors
compare_distributions <- function(train_data, classify_data) {
  common_vars <- intersect(colnames(train_data), colnames(classify_data))
  train_data <- train_data[, common_vars, drop = FALSE]
  classify_data <- classify_data[, common_vars, drop = FALSE]
  
  results <- data.frame(
    Predictor = character(),
    JSD = numeric(),
    JSD_Interpretation = character(),
    TVD = numeric(),
    TVD_Interpretation = character(),
    Overall_Interpretation = character(),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  for (predictor in common_vars) {
    p <- normalize(train_data[[predictor]])
    q <- normalize(classify_data[[predictor]])
    
    jsd <- calculate_jsd(p, q)
    tv <- calculate_tv(p, q)
    
    jsd_int <- interpret_jsd(jsd)
    tv_int <- interpret_tv(tv)
    overall <- overall_interpretation(jsd_int, tv_int)
    
    results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
      Predictor = predictor,
      JSD = jsd,
      JSD_Interpretation = jsd_int,
      TVD = tv,
      TVD_Interpretation = tv_int,
      Overall_Interpretation = overall,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }

  # Add overall summary row
  avg_jsd <- mean(results$JSD, na.rm = TRUE)
  avg_tv <- mean(results$TVD, na.rm = TRUE)
  avg_jsd_int <- interpret_jsd(avg_jsd)
  avg_tv_int <- interpret_tv(avg_tv)
  avg_overall <- overall_interpretation(avg_jsd_int, avg_tv_int)

  summary_row <- data.frame(
    Predictor = "OVERALL",
    JSD = avg_jsd,
    JSD_Interpretation = avg_jsd_int,
    TVD = avg_tv,
    TVD_Interpretation = avg_tv_int,
    Overall_Interpretation = avg_overall,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  results <- rbind(results, summary_row)
  return(results)
}

LOD_detection <- function(thresholds_df, classify) {
  # Step 1: Find common variables
  common_vars <- intersect(colnames(thresholds_df), colnames(classify))
  
  # Step 2: Ensure numeric comparison
  classify_numeric <- as.data.frame(lapply(classify[common_vars], as.numeric))
  thresholds_numeric <- as.numeric(thresholds_df[1, common_vars])
  
  # Step 3: Check values below threshold
  below_threshold <- mapply(function(col, threshold) {
    col < threshold
  }, classify_numeric, thresholds_numeric, SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
  
  below_threshold_df <- as.data.frame(below_threshold)
  
  # Step 4: Calculate percentage of TRUEs (below threshold)
  percent_true_per_row <- rowMeans(below_threshold_df, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  
  # Step 5: Calculate percentage of zeros
  percent_zeros_df <- as.data.frame(lapply(classify_numeric, function(col) col == 0))
  percent_zeros_per_row <- rowMeans(percent_zeros_df, na.rm = TRUE) * 100
  
  # Step 6: Return result with sample ID (assumed to be in first column of classify)
  result <- data.frame(
    ID = classify[[1]],
    LOD = percent_true_per_row,
    Zeros = percent_zeros_per_row
  )
  
  return(result)
}
```




# Choose the files with the data. Decide on the path for the dilution simulation. Collect the descriptive statistics.
## Selection of the training file

The user is prompted to select the training data file, ensuring the dataset is properly structured:

- **Column headings** should indicate variable names, with the class in the first column.
- **Row 1**: Quantitative (1) or qualitative (0) variable.
- **Row 2**: Detection limit (cfus, pfps, gcs, etc.).
- **Row 3**: MST marker (1) or not (0).


| Class    | Parameter 1 | Parameter 2 | Parameter 3 |
|----------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
|          | 1           | 1           | 0           |
|          | 95          | 19          | 0.001       |
|          | 1           | 1           | 0           |
| HUMAN    | 101         | 2523        | 1           |
| POULTRY  | 17090       | 125         | 0           |
| BOVINE   | 254         | 242         | 0           |
| PORCINE  | 327         | 0           | 0           |

For more details, refer to the help section.

## Selection of subrutine for dilutions 
MST parameters are usually found in highly contaminated stool or water samples, like those from abattoir sewage or urban wastewater treatment plants. However, it's sometimes necessary to identify contamination sources in samples with fewer MST parameters. Simulating a dilution process can help improve classification accuracy in machine learning training, especially when direct measurement is difficult due to low concentrations or interference.

Ichnaea-MST uses two Monte Carlo simulation methods for this. The first method simulates the relationship between the presence of a parameter in the contamination source and a similar matrix that needs classification. The second method simulates various dilution levels, from none to the maximum specified by the user, to understand how dilution affects MST parameter detection and classification. This helps create robust machine learning models that can accurately predict contamination sources even in complex conditions.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Display a message dialog explaining the simulation of a dilution process for increasing sample numbers for machine classification
svDialogs::dlg_message('To simulate a dilution process to increase the number of samples for machine classification, select your desired settings carefully, as this choice cannot be changed later. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res

repeat {
  # Display an input dialog asking if a file containing the occurrence of a "parameter model" is available
svDialogs::dlgInput('Please indicate whether you have data corresponding to the presence or occurrence of a marker that can be used to estimate dilution. Please note that two occurrences are required: the source of the contamination and the target matrix. If not, a random dilution simulation will be performed. Could you please confirm whether the file is available in a compatible format (y/n)?', password = TRUE)$res->doyouwant
  
 # Check if the user input is valid (either 'y', 'Y', 'n', or 'N')
  if (doyouwant %in% c('y', 'Y', 'n', 'N')) {
    break
  } else {
    # Prompt the user to enter a valid response if the input is invalid
    svDialogs::dlg_message('Please enter a valid response. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res
  }
}


# Set manual.dilution to 'n' if the user indicates the file is available
selected.dilution.fold<-0
if (tolower(doyouwant) == 'y'){manual.dilution='n'}
if (tolower(doyouwant) == 'n'){manual.dilution='y'}

# If the user indicates the file is not available, proceed with the following steps
if (tolower(doyouwant) != 'y'){
    # Display a message dialog explaining the importance of understanding MST parameter dilution during data augmentation
  svDialogs::dlg_message('When augmenting data, it is crucial to understand how much the MST parameters are diluted within the designated matrix. Excessive dilution is not recommended. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res  

  # Display a message dialog requesting the estimation of the maximum dilution fold for MST markers
  svDialogs::dlg_message('Please enter the maximum dilution fold for the MST markers in the target matrix as an integer, without periods or commas. If your training data are in logarithmic values, express the dilution rate as a logarithm. The program will use the provided maximum dilution rate without knowing if your values are logarithmic. For example, 3 logs of dilution equal 10000. In southern European surface waters, a maximum dilution of 10000 to 15000 allows MST parameter classification. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res      

  # Repeat the process of asking for the dilution fold until the user confirms their selection
  repeat {
    user_input <- svDialogs::dlgInput('Indicate the dilution maximun dilution fold', password = TRUE)$res
        # Validate the input
    if (!is.na(as.numeric(user_input)) && as.numeric(user_input)>0 ) {
      dilution.fold <- as.numeric(user_input)
      svDialogs::dlg_message(paste('Your maximum dilution value is: ', dilution.fold, '. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.'))$res 
      selected.dilution.fold<-1
      break
    } else {svDialogs::dlg_message('That is an invalid value. Please enter a valid value')$res}
  }
  
}

# If the user did not confirm the manual dilution, proceed with the following steps
if (tolower(manual.dilution) != 'y') {
  # Display a message dialog prompting the user to indicate the file containing the marker data for augmentation
  svDialogs::dlg_message('Please select the file containing the data with the occurrences that will be used in the augmentation process. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res
  
  # Open a file dialog for the user to select the dataset for the dilution simulation, allowing all file types
  svDialogs::dlg_open(title = "Select the dataset for the dilution simulation", filters = svDialogs::dlg_filters[c('All'), ])$res->todilute
  
  # Import the selected data and convert it into a data frame
  todilute<-as.data.frame(import_data(todilute))
}
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
    svDialogs::dlg_message('The data file has been generated with the name LOD_Zero_table.dta. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res
  }    
  
  if (doyouwant=='5' ){
    file_path <- 'LOD_Zero_table.sav'
    save_data(lod_zeros, file_path)
    svDialogs::dlg_message('The data file has been generated with the name LOD_Zero_table.sav. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res
  }
}
}
```

### In the event that a t90 amendment is employed for the purpose of modifying classification
Please select the file containing the dataset with natural decays, specifically the t90 values. The t90 represents the time needed for a 1 log (90%) decay of the initial occurrence. Next, indicate the time of persistence you wish to simulate, using the same units as the t90 values. This helps model the decay behavior of MST markers accurately. The entered time is taken as the residence time, modifying the classification dataset values based on natural decay rates. This adjustment ensures the dataset reflects the extended duration of parameter persistence. Note that some decays are temperature-dependent, and different t90 values for the same MST marker may be reported in the literature.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Display a message dialog explaining the prompt for indicating the availability of a file for t90-based decays, if not a manual dilution will be set

    break
  } else {
    svDialogs::dlg_message('Please enter a valid response. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res
  }
}

# If the user indicates the t90 file is available, proceed with the following steps
if (tolower(t90_amendment) == 'y') {
  # Display a message dialog prompting the user to select the file containing the t90 data
  svDialogs::dlg_message('Please select the file that contains the t90 data. To proceed, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res
  
  # Open a file dialog for the user to select the dataset containing the t90 values, allowing all file types
  svDialogs::dlg_open(title = "Select the dataset containing the t90 values", filters = svDialogs::dlg_filters[c('All'), ])$res->t90s
  
  # Import the selected data and convert it into a data frame
  t90s<-as.data.frame(import_data(t90s))
}
```

# Data augmentation
This section explains the data augmentation process, which is essential for machine learning classification. Ichnaea-MST uses resampling techniques and simulated dilution to create artificial samples, enriching the dataset. Quantitative markers, assumed to follow a Poisson distribution, show greater variability after simulated dilution. Qualitative samples are directly subjected to dilution.

Detection of MST markers depends on whether values are above or below detection limits for quantitative samples, or detection thresholds for qualitative samples. After resampling, samples are added to the original dataset, repeating the process as needed based on the complexity of the training dataset. The number of samples required depends on the number of MST markers and classes to be classified.

This section outlines the functions for the two types of data augmentation in Ichnaea-MST.



## Defined function when no dilutions markers are available
This function uses a random dilution factor resampling technique, selecting from dilution factors between 1 (undiluted) and the maximum value specified by the user.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# This part is for dilution as is indicated by the user 
  dilution.m<-function(replicas, data, dilution.fold){
    # Extract the first three rows and all columns except the first from 'data', and assign to 'metadata'
    data[c(1, 2, 3), -1]->metadata
    data<-data[c(-1, -2, -3), ]
    row.names(data)<-NULL
    
    # Identify column names in 'metadata' where the first row contains the value 1, and assign to 'quantitatives'
    quantitatives<-names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[1, ])])
    
    # Identify column names in 'metadata' where the first row contains the value 0, and assign to 'qualitatives'
    qualitatives<-names(metadata[, grep(0, metadata[1, ])])
    
    # Sampling and dilution
    n.seq<-replicas
    data2<-data
    diluted<-1/runif(replicas, 1, as.numeric(dilution.fold))
    dilution.fraction<-sample(diluted, 1)
    data[, quantitatives]->df1
    data[, qualitatives]->df2
    data$Class->df0
    
    # Initialize temporary data frames for quantitative and qualitative columns
    if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
      matrix(nrow=1, ncol=length(quantitatives))->df1.temp
      as.data.frame(df1.temp)->df1.temp
      names(df1.temp)<-names(df1)
    }
    if (length(qualitatives)!=0){
      matrix(nrow=1, ncol=length(qualitatives))->df2.temp
      as.data.frame(df2.temp)->df2.temp
      names(df2.temp)<-names(df2)
    }
    matrix(nrow=1, ncol=1)->df0.temp
    as.data.frame(df0.temp)->df0.temp

    
    # Perform dilution for the specified number of replicas
    for (i in seq(1, n.seq, 1)) {
      if (length(quantitatives)!=0){data[, quantitatives]->df1}
      if (length(qualitatives)!=0){data[, qualitatives]->df2}
      data$Class->df0
      if (length(quantitatives)!=0){row.n<-sample(nrow(df1), 1)}
      if (length(qualitatives)!=0){row.n<-sample(nrow(df2), 1)}
      
      if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
        for (t in 1:length(quantitatives)){
          a<-rpois(1, df1[row.n, t])
          df1.temp[1, t]<-a*dilution.fraction
        }
      }
      if (length(qualitatives)!=0){
        for (t in 1:length(qualitatives)){
          a<-df2[row.n, t]
          df2.temp[1, t]<-a*dilution.fraction
        }
      }
      df0.temp<-df0[row.n]
      if (length(qualitatives)==0){cbind(df0.temp, df1.temp)->data.temp}
      if (length(quantitatives)==0){cbind(df0.temp, df2.temp)->data.temp}
      if (length(quantitatives)!=0 & length(qualitatives)!=0) {cbind(df0.temp, df1.temp, df2.temp)->data.temp}
      names(data.temp)<-c('Class', names(data.temp[, -1]))
      data2 <- rbind(data2, data.temp)
    }
    
    # Recodification according to detection limit
    if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
      data2[quantitatives]->data2.q
      metadata[quantitatives]->metadata.q
    }
    if (length(qualitatives)!=0){
      data2[qualitatives]->data2.ql
      metadata[qualitatives]->metadata.ql
    }
    if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
      for(i in 1:length(names(data2.q))){
        data2.q[, i][data2.q[, i]<=metadata.q[2, i]]<-0
      }
    }
    if (length(qualitatives)!=0){
      for(i in 1:length(names(data2.ql))){
        data2.ql[, i][data2.ql[, i]<=metadata.ql[2, i]]<-0
        data2.ql[, i][data2.ql[, i]!=0]<-1
      }
    }
    # Combination of the variables
    if (length(qualitatives)==0){data3<-cbind(data2$Class, data2.q)}
    if (length(quantitatives)==0){data3<-cbind(data2$Class, data2.ql)}
    if (length(quantitatives)!=0 & length(qualitatives)!=0) {data3<-cbind(data2$Class, data2.q, data2.ql)}
    names(data3)<-c('Class', names(data3[, -1]))
    return(data3)
  }
```



## Defined function when two dilutions markers are available
This function uses a dilution factor obtained by resampling possible dilution ratios based on the probability densities of two markers. The user should indicate any potential discrepancies between the actual marker data in the matrix to be classified and the simulated marker values in the augmented dataset.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# This part is for the dilution using the two 'dilution' markers
  dilution<-function(replicas, todilute, data){
    # Extract the first three rows and all columns except the first from 'data', and assign to 'metadata'
    data[c(1, 2, 3), -1]->metadata
    data<-data[c(-1, -2, -3), ]
    row.names(data)<-NULL
    
    # Identify column names in 'metadata' where the first row contains the value 1, and assign to 'quantitatives'
    quantitatives<-names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[1, ])])
    
    # Identify column names in 'metadata' where the first row contains the value 0, and assign to 'qualitatives'
    qualitatives<-names(metadata[, grep(0, metadata[1, ])])
    
    # Extract origin and target densities from 'todilute'
    origin_d<-todilute[, grep(0, todilute[1, ])]
    target_d<-todilute[, grep(1, todilute[1, ])]
    
    origin_d[-c(1, 2)]->origin_density
    target_d[-c(1, 2)]->target_density
    origin_d[2]->dl.origin_d
    target_d[2]->dl.target_d
    
    as.data.frame(na.omit(origin_d[-c(1, 2)]))->origin_dd
    as.data.frame(na.omit(target_d[-c(1, 2)]))->target_dd
    names(origin_dd)<-c(names(todilute)[grep(0, todilute[1, ])])
    names(target_dd)<-names(todilute)[grep(1, todilute[1, ])]
    
    # Sampling and dilution
    n.seq<-replicas
    data2<-data
    
    density(na.omit(origin_density), bw='SJ', from=min(na.omit(origin_density)), to=max(na.omit(origin_density)))->densidad_0
    density(na.omit(target_density), bw='SJ', from=min(na.omit(target_density)), to=max(na.omit(target_density)))->densidad_1
    
    library(mc2d)
    mcstoc(rempiricalD, values=densidad_0$x, prob=densidad_0$y, nsv=replicas, rtrunc=T, linf=0)->target_0
    mcstoc(rempiricalD, values=densidad_1$x, prob=densidad_1$y, nsv=replicas, rtrunc=T, linf=0)->target_1
    
    diluted<-as.numeric((target_1/target_0))
    dilution.fraction<-sample(diluted, 1)
    
    data[, quantitatives]->df1
    data[, qualitatives]->df2
    
    # Define variables origin and target, this last will be used to validate the simulation of the dilution process
    as.numeric(unlist(origin_dd))->origin_ddd
    as.numeric(unlist(target_dd))->target_ddd
    data$Class->df0
    
    # Initialize temporary data frames for quantitative, qualitative and target and origin variables
    if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
      matrix(nrow=1, ncol=length(quantitatives))->df1.temp
      matrix(nrow=1, ncol=1)->origin_d.temp
      matrix(nrow=1, ncol=1)->target_d.temp
      as.data.frame(df1.temp)->df1.temp
      as.data.frame(origin_d.temp)->origin_d.temp
      as.data.frame(target_d.temp)->target_d.temp
      names(df1.temp)<-names(df1)
      names(origin_d.temp)<-names(origin_d)
      names(target_d.temp)<-names(target_d)
    }
    
    if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
      matrix(nrow=1, ncol=length(qualitatives))->df2.temp
      matrix(nrow=1, ncol=1)->origin_d.temp
      matrix(nrow=1, ncol=1)->target_d.temp 
      as.data.frame(df2.temp)->df2.temp
      as.data.frame(origin_d.temp)->origin_d.temp
      as.data.frame(target_d.temp)->target_d.temp
      names(df2.temp)<-names(df2)
      names(origin_d.temp)<-names(origin_d)
      names(target_d.temp)<-names(target_d)
    }
    
    matrix(nrow=1, ncol=1)->df0.temp
    as.data.frame(df0.temp)->df0.temp
    
    # Perform dilution for the specified number of replicas
    for (i in seq(1, n.seq, 1)) {
      if (length(quantitatives)!=0){data[, quantitatives]->df1}
      if (length(qualitatives)!=0){data[, qualitatives]->df2}
      data$Class->df0
      
      if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
        row.n<-sample(nrow(df1), 1)
        row.n1<-sample(nrow(as.data.frame(origin_dd)), 1)
        row.n2<-sample(nrow(as.data.frame(target_dd)), 1)
      }
      
      if (length(qualitatives)!=0){
        row.n<-sample(nrow(df2), 1)
        row.n1<-sample(nrow(as.data.frame(origin_dd)), 1)
        row.n2<-sample(nrow(as.data.frame(target_dd)), 1)
      }
      
      if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
        for (t in 1:length(quantitatives)){
          a<-rpois(1, df1[row.n, t])
          df1.temp[1, t]<-a*dilution.fraction
        }
        a1<-rpois(1, origin_dd[row.n1, ])
        a2<-rpois(1, target_dd[row.n2, ])
        origin_d.temp[1]<-a1*dilution.fraction
        target_d.temp[1]<-a2*dilution.fraction
      }
      
      if (length(qualitatives)!=0){
        for (t in 1:length(qualitatives)){
          a<-df2[row.n, t]
          df2.temp[1, t]<-a*dilution.fraction
        }
        a1<-rpois(1, origin_dd[row.n1, ])
        a2<-rpois(1, target_dd[row.n2, ])
        origin_d.temp[1]<-a1*dilution.fraction
        target_d.temp[1]<-a2*dilution.fraction
      }
      
      df0.temp<-df0[row.n]
      if (length(qualitatives)==0){cbind(df0.temp, df1.temp)->data.temp}
      if (length(quantitatives)==0){cbind(df0.temp, df2.temp)->data.temp}
      if (length(quantitatives)!=0 & length(qualitatives)!=0) {cbind(df0.temp, df1.temp, df2.temp)->data.temp}
      names(data.temp)<-c('Class', names(data.temp[, -1]))
      rbind(data2, data.temp)->data2
      c(origin_ddd, as.numeric(origin_d.temp))->origin_ddd
      c(target_ddd, as.numeric(target_d.temp))->target_ddd
    }
    
    as.data.frame(origin_ddd)->origin_ddd
    as.data.frame(target_ddd)->target_ddd
    names(origin_ddd)<-names(origin_dd)
    names(target_ddd)<-names(origin_dd)
    
    # Recodification according to detection limit
    if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
      data2[quantitatives]->data2.q
      metadata[quantitatives]->metadata.q
    }
    if (length(qualitatives)!=0){
      data2[qualitatives]->data2.ql
      metadata[qualitatives]->metadata.ql
    }
    if (length(quantitatives)!=0){
      for(i in 1:length(names(data2.q))){
        data2.q[, i][data2.q[, i]<=metadata.q[2, i]]<-0
      }
      origin_ddd[origin_ddd<=dl.origin_d]<-0
      target_ddd[target_ddd<=dl.target_d]<-0
    }
    
    if (length(qualitatives)!=0){
      for(i in 1:length(names(data2.ql))){
        data2.ql[, i][data2.ql[, i]<=metadata.ql[2, i]]<-0
        data2.ql[, i][data2.ql[, i]!=0]<-1
      }
      origin_ddd[origin_ddd<=dl.origin_d]<-0
      target_ddd[target_ddd<=dl.target_d]<-0
    }
    
    # Combination fo the variables 
    if (length(qualitatives)==0){data3<-cbind(data2$Class, data2.q)}
    if (length(quantitatives)==0){data3<-cbind(data2$Class, data2.ql)}
    if (length(quantitatives)!=0 & length(qualitatives)!=0) {data3<-cbind(data2$Class, data2.q, data2.ql)}
    names(data3)<-c('Class', names(data3[, -1]))
    return(list(data3, origin_ddd, target_ddd))
  }

```



# Information window about the number of classes, MST markers, number of samples and the number of replicas needed based on the power analysis for the model  
This section calculates the number of replications needed for a study using power analysis with the pwr package. Power analysis helps determine the sample size required to detect an effect with a specified confidence level. The code uses the pwr.f2.test function to calculate the sample size needed for a statistical power of 0.9 (90%).

Increasing the minimum number of replicas improves the model's accuracy and statistical power by providing more training data. However, this also increases computational demands and training time. Additionally, non-representative or noisy data can lead to overfitting. By default, the minimum number of replicas is increased by a factor of five.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Calculate the number of replicas needed based on the power analysis for the model
replicas<-1+as.numeric(pwr::pwr.f2.test(u = length(names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[3,])])), f2 = 0.02, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.9)[1])+as.numeric(pwr::pwr.f2.test(u = length(names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[3,])])), f2 = 0.02, sig.level = 0.05, power = 0.9)[2])
round(replicas, 0)->replicas

replicas.purged<-5*replicas

if (tolower(manual.dilution) != 'y') {
replicas.purged<-5*replicas+1*length((todilute[, grep(0, todilute[1, ])]))-2}

# Create a message detailing the model's characteristics and the required sample size for augmentation
paste('Your model has ', length(unique(na.omit(data$Class))), ' classes ', 'and ', length(names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[3, ])])), ' MST-markers ', ' with ', length(na.omit(data$Class)), ' samples.', ' In consideration of the characteristics inherent to your model, a minimum sample size of ', replicas, ' samples may be appropriate.', ' Accordingly, an augmented dataset will be generated by concatenating five replicates with the minimum number. Once the simulation is complete, the expected number of samples will be about ', replicas.purged, '.', ' The 70 % of these samples ' , round(0.7*replicas.purged, 0), ' will be used for training and the remaining ', round(0.3*replicas.purged, 0), ' samples for validation. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.', sep='')->text.dialog

# Display the message dialog with the generated text to show the info
svDialogs::dlg_message(text.dialog)$res

```



# Dataset for data augmentation & Amendment of the augmented dataset
In this section, the augmented dataset is generated by parallelizing the data augmentation function and launching five threads simultaneously. The original training samples are included only once in the augmented dataset.

When incorporating the data of the two markers for dilution, a dialog box prompts the user for the maximum discrepancy between the dilution marker's occurrence in the target matrix and the augmented dataset. If the desired discrepancy level isn't achieved after ten attempts, the user is directed to select the maximum dilution level.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# If manual dilution is not selected, proceed with the following steps
if (tolower(manual.dilution) != 'y') {

# Dialog box to introduce this stage  
    svDialogs::dlg_message('Next, the simulation of contamination dilution will begin, based on empirical density (empirical probability density). This method estimates the probability distribution of a marker in the contamination origin matrix and a similar matrix to be classified, using observed data without assuming a theoretical distribution. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res  
  
# Dialog box  
    svDialogs::dlg_message('In the next stage, you will be prompted to indicate the maximum difference between the medians of the two "dilution markers". These medians come from the dilution simulation of the marker in the contamination origin, not the real values in the target matrix. Note that closer medians require more computations. If adjustment is not feasible after 10 runs, an estimated dilution ratio will be used, and the program will continue. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res

# Introduce the mean threshold
  svDialogs::dlgInput('Please specify the acceptable log10 difference between the medians, a value of 0.5 would be fine. Please introduce a valid value.', password = TRUE)$res->user_input
  
  # Validate the input
if (!is.na(as.numeric(user_input))) {
  break.level <- as.numeric(user_input)
  svDialogs::dlg_message(paste('Your threshold is: ', break.level, 'log 10. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.'))$res
} else {
  svDialogs::dlg_message('That is an invalid value. Please enter a valid value')$res
  }
  
  # Initialise a counter
  counter<-0
  
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(doParallel))
  cl <- makePSOCKcluster(detectCores())
  registerDoParallel(cl)
  
  repeat {
    # Execute the foreach loop to obtain the three lists (MST data and how markers for dilution are diluted, target_dd can be omitted)
    results <- foreach(i = 1:5, .combine = 'list', .multicombine = TRUE) %dopar% {
      dilution(replicas, todilute, data)
    }
    
    # Initialize lists to store the results
    data_list <- list()
    origin_dd_list <- list()
    target_dd_list <- list()
    
    # Separate the results into the corresponding lists
    for (i in 1:length(results)) {
      data_list[[i]] <- results[[i]][[1]]
      origin_dd_list[[i]] <- results[[i]][[2]]
      target_dd_list[[i]] <- results[[i]][[3]]
    }
    
    # Combine the results of each list
    data3_combined <- do.call(rbind, data_list)
    origin_dd_combined <- do.call(rbind, origin_dd_list)
    target_dd_combined <- do.call(rbind, target_dd_list)
    
    data3_combined->data3
    
    # Function to remove repeated dataset from origin MST samples in the final data augmentation
    rem.repats<-function(Training, Simulated){
      length(Training[, 1])-3->longitud
      remove<-c(seq(replicas+longitud+1, replicas+2*longitud, 1), seq(2*replicas+2*longitud+1, 2*replicas+3*longitud, 1), seq(3*replicas+3*longitud+1, 3*replicas+4*longitud, 1), seq(4*replicas+4*longitud+1, 4*replicas+5*longitud, 1))
      return(Simulated[-remove, ])
    }
    rem.repats(data, data3)->data3
    
    real.target <- as.numeric(na.omit(unlist(todilute[grep(1, todilute[1, ])])))
    simulated.target <- as.numeric(unlist(origin_dd_combined))
    
    max_length <- max(length(real.target), length(simulated.target))
    real.target <- c(real.target, rep(NA, max_length - length(real.target)))
    simulated.target <- c(simulated.target, rep(NA, max_length - length(simulated.target)))
    
    targets <- data.frame(Real = real.target, Simulated = simulated.target)
    
    # Break the loop if the median log10 difference is within the acceptable range (per default ± 0.5 log10)
    
    counter<-counter+1
    
    print(counter) # this line can be safely removed
    
    if (abs(median(log10(targets$Simulated+1)- median(na.omit(log10(targets$Real+1)))))<=break.level) {break}
    if (counter==10) {manual.dilution='y'}
    if (counter==10){svDialogs::dlg_message('It was impossible to obtain a valid diference after 10 runs. It will proceed with a dilution ratio. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res}
    if (counter==10) {break}
  }
  stopCluster(cl)
  registerDoSEQ()
  
  if (tolower(manual.dilution) != 'y') {
  # Create and save a comparison boxplot between real and simulated targets
  par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
  boxplot(log10(targets+1), names=c('Real', 'Simulated'), main=substitute(paste(bold('Boxplot'))), ylab=expression('Log'[10]*'(values + 1)'), col=c('lightblue', 'lightgreen'))

  plot(density(na.omit(log10(targets+1)$Real)), main=substitute(paste(bold('Density plot'))), xlab=expression('Log'[10]*'(values + 1)'), col='lightblue', lwd=2, xlim=c(min(c(na.omit(log10(targets+1)$Real), log10(na.omit(simulated.target+1)))), max(c(na.omit(log10(targets+1)$Real)), log10(na.omit(simulated.target+1)))))
  
lines(density(log10(na.omit(simulated.target+1))), col='lightgreen', lwd=2)
  
  jpeg('Comparison boxplot between real and simulated.jpeg', res=600, width = 8, height = 5, units = 'in')
  par(mfrow=c(1, 2))
  boxplot(log10(targets+1), names=c('Real', 'Simulated'), main=substitute(paste(bold('Boxplot'))), ylab=expression('Log'[10]*'(values + 1)'), col=c('lightblue', 'lightgreen'))

  plot(density(na.omit(log10(targets+1)$Real)), main=substitute(paste(bold('Density plot'))), xlab=expression('Log'[10]*'(values + 1)'), col='lightblue', lwd=2, xlim=c(min(c(na.omit(log10(targets+1)$Real), log10(na.omit(simulated.target+1)))), max(c(na.omit(log10(targets+1)$Real)), log10(na.omit(simulated.target+1)))))
  
lines(density(log10(na.omit(simulated.target+1))), col='lightgreen', lwd=2)
  dev.off()
}
}


# If manual dilution is selected, proceed with the following steps
if (tolower(manual.dilution) == 'y' & selected.dilution.fold == 0) {

# Display a message dialog explaining the importance of understanding MST parameter dilution during data augmentation
  svDialogs::dlg_message('When augmenting data, it is crucial to understand how much the MST parameters are diluted within the designated matrix. Excessive dilution is not recommended. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res  

  # Display a message dialog requesting the estimation of the maximum dilution fold for MST markers
  svDialogs::dlg_message('Please indicate the maximum dilution fold for the MST markers in the target matrix as an integer, without periods or commas. If all training data are logarithmic values, express the dilution rate as a logarithm. Note that the program will handle the maximum dilution rate as provided, without knowing if your values are logarithmic. For example, 3 logs of dilution equal 10000. In southern European surface waters, a maximum dilution of 10000 to 15000 allows MST parameter classification. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res      

  # Repeat the process of asking for the dilution fold until the user confirms their selection
  repeat {
    user_input <- svDialogs::dlgInput('Indicate the dilution maximun dilution fold', password = TRUE)$res
        # Validate the input
    if (!is.na(as.numeric(user_input)) && as.numeric(user_input)>0 ) {
      dilution.fold <- as.numeric(user_input)
      svDialogs::dlg_message(paste('Your maximum dilution value is: ', dilution.fold, '. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.'))$res 
      break
    } else {svDialogs::dlg_message('That is an invalid value. Please enter a valid value')$res}
  } 
  
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(doParallel))
  cl <- makePSOCKcluster(detectCores())
  registerDoParallel(cl)
  
  data3<-foreach(i = 1:5, .combine = 'rbind') %dopar% {dilution.m(replicas, data, dilution.fold)}
  
  # Function to remove repeated samples
  rem.repats<-function(Training, Simulated){
    length(Training[, 1])-3->longitud
    remove<-c(seq(replicas+longitud+1, replicas+2*longitud, 1), seq(2*replicas+2*longitud+1, 2*replicas+3*longitud, 1), seq(3*replicas+3*longitud+1, 3*replicas+4*longitud, 1), seq(4*replicas+4*longitud+1, 4*replicas+5*longitud, 1))
    return(Simulated[-remove, ])
  }
  rem.repats(data, data3)->data3
  
  stopCluster(cl)
  registerDoSEQ()
}

# If manual dilution is selected, proceed with the following steps
if (tolower(manual.dilution) == 'y' & selected.dilution.fold != 0) {

# Display a message dialog explaining the importance of understanding MST parameter dilution during data augmentation
  svDialogs::dlg_message(paste('The augmentation with a dilution fold of: ', dilution.fold, ' is going to start. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.'))$res 

  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(doParallel))
  cl <- makePSOCKcluster(detectCores())
  registerDoParallel(cl)
  
  data3<-foreach(i = 1:5, .combine = 'rbind') %dopar% {dilution.m(replicas, data, dilution.fold)}
  
  # Function to remove repeated samples
  rem.repats<-function(Training, Simulated){
    length(Training[, 1])-3->longitud
    remove<-c(seq(replicas+longitud+1, replicas+2*longitud, 1), seq(2*replicas+2*longitud+1, 2*replicas+3*longitud, 1), seq(3*replicas+3*longitud+1, 3*replicas+4*longitud, 1), seq(4*replicas+4*longitud+1, 4*replicas+5*longitud, 1))
    return(Simulated[-remove, ])
  }
  rem.repats(data, data3)->data3
  
  stopCluster(cl)
  registerDoSEQ()
}
```

# Exportation of the augmented dataset to a file
It is proposed that some parameters for MST are relationships between two parameters, such as the ratio of log10 values between somatic coliphages and the GA17 bacteriophage of _Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron_. The R script would process this ratio as an additional parameter, but this is incorrect. To address this issue, a methodology has been formulated.

This methodology involves the use of a file to store the outcomes of the data augmentation table. Furthermore, it allows the user to make any alterations they deem appropriate and subsequently incorporate them into the program.

It is imperative to recreate the headers of the first three rows; however, in this instance, the detection limit value or the nature of the variable will not be considered, yet the values of the third row will be taken into account.

Consider the ratio of log10 values between somatic coliphages and the GA17 bacteriophage of _B. thetaiotaomicron_. It is evident that coliphages do not serve as MST markers, given their excretion by humans and animals. Consequently, the metadata associated with this parameter could be:

- **Row 1**: 1
- **Row 2**: 10
- **Row 3**: 0 

(_quantitative variable, detection limit of 10 pfus/100mL, not a predictor in training_)

For the bacteriophage of _B. thetaiotaomicron_ (very specific to humans), its metadata could be:

- **Row 1**: 1
- **Row 2**: 10
- **Row 3**: 1

(_quantitative variable, detection limit of 0 pfus/100mL, predictor in training_)

For the ratio, its metadata could be:

- **Row 1**: 1
- **Row 2**: 0
- **Row 3**: 1 

(_quantitative variable, detection limit of 0, predictor in training_)




# Machine learning

Machine learning can be categorized into three types: **supervised learning**, **unsupervised learning**, and **reinforcement learning**. MST classification falls under supervised learning, as it involves training an algorithm on labeled data. This process includes categorizing contamination types into classes like human, non-human, poultry, bovine, equine, etc., or as a percentage of a specific contamination type. The first categorization is a classification problem, while the second is a regression problem.

H2O AutoML uses various supervised learning algorithms for classification and regression tasks, including:

- **Generalized Linear Models (GLM)**
- **Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM)**
- **Distributed Random Forest (DRF)**
- **Deep Learning (Neural Networks)**
- **eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost)**
- **Stacked Ensembles**

Each algorithm has its strengths. The training process is computationally demanding, with Deep Learning, XGBoost, and Stacked Ensembles being the most demanding, and GLM the least. Tree-based models (DRF, GBM, and XGBoost) are optimal for interpreting training outcomes. H2O AutoML trains multiple model types, automatically tuning and evaluating them to find the best model for a dataset.

GBM is the default option for training due to its optimized implementation by H2O.

Machine learning is a probabilistic process, meaning results can vary even with the same augmented dataset. Factors like random initialization, training and validation dataset creation, and hyperparameter tuning can influence model selection. It's crucial to consider multiple runs and evaluations to ensure robust and reliable model performance.



```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Display a message dialog box with information about Ichanea-MST machine learning
svDialogs::dlg_message('Ichanea-MST offers several options
training options with different families of machine learning algorithms. The default option is the use of GBM (https://docs.h2o.ai/h2o/latest-stable/h2o-docs/data-science/gbm.html). In addition, Ichanea-MST implements the MST-markers reduction option. Subsequently you will be asked if you want to run this optimisation (https://docs.h2o.ai/h2o/latest-stable/h2o-r/docs/reference/h2o.infogram.html). To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res
```


## Training process
In this section, the user selects the algorithms for training and the number of models to evaluate. The augmented dataset is then split into two parts: 70% for training and 30% for validation.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Check if 'new.augmented' is set to 1. This means that an augmented dataset has been created.
if (new.augmented==1){
  # Assign new data to variables
  data3 <- new.data3  
  metadata <- new.metadata
  quantitatives <- new.quantitatives
  qualitatives <- new.qualitatives
}

# Suppress package startup messages
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(h2o))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(caret))

# Display a message dialog box about configuring default options for automatic machine learning
svDialogs::dlg_message('Now we will start configuring the default options for an automatic machine learning. To proceed, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res

# Display a message dialog box about the computational demands of certain models
svDialogs::dlg_message('Note that Deep Learning, eXtreme Gradient Boosting (only works under Linux) and Stacked Ensemble models are highly computer demanding.')$res

# Repeat loop to get user input for model selection
# Define available algorithms

# Display input dialog
library(svDialogs)

repeat {
  # Prompt user for input
svDialogs::dlgInput('Please indicate your preferred algorithm(s): (1) Distributed Random Forest (DRF) and Extremely Randomised Trees (XRT); (2) Generalised Linear Model with regularisation (GLM); (3) eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost); (4 - default) Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM); (5) Deep Learning models; and (6) Stacked Ensemble models. Please select one or more algorithms (1 to 6) by entering their numbers, separated by commas or spaces.',password = TRUE)$res-> doyouwant 

  # Clean and split input
  selected <- unlist(strsplit(gsub(",", " ", doyouwant), "\\s+"))
  selected <- selected[selected != ""]  # Remove empty strings

  # Check if all inputs are valid
  if (all(selected %in% as.character(1:6))) {
    # Check if only option 3 is selected and OS is Windows
    if (length(selected) == 1 && selected == "3" && .Platform$OS.type == "windows") {
      svDialogs::dlg_message('Please be advised that selecting XGBoost alone is not currently an option in Windows.')$res} else {break}
  } 
  else {svDialogs::dlg_message("Invalid input. Please enter numbers from 1 to 6, separated by commas or spaces.")$res}
}

# Map selections to algorithm names
algo_map <- c('DRF', 'GLM', 'XGBoost', 'GBM', 'DeepLearning', 'StackedEnsemble')
algo <- algo_map[as.integer(selected)]

# Repeat loop to get user input for the number of models to be tested
repeat {
  # Display input dialog box for the number of models
  svDialogs::dlgInput('Please indicate how many models should be tested. By default 50 is a good choice for binary classification or 25 for multiclass classification.', password = TRUE)$res -> doyouwant
  
  num_input <- as.numeric(doyouwant)
  # Check if the input is a valid number
  if (!is.na(num_input) && num_input > 0) {
    break
  } else {
    # Display message dialog box for invalid input
    svDialogs::dlg_message('Please enter a valid response. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res
  }
}

# Assign the number of models to be tested to variable model_number
model_number <- as.numeric(doyouwant)

# Selection of variables
data3[names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[3, ])])] -> data4
# If we remove row 3 from metadata, assign data3 to data4 (left as a precaution)
data4$Class <- data3$Class

# Split samples into training and validation sets
inTrain <- createDataPartition(y = data4$Class, p = .70, list = FALSE)
training <- data4[inTrain, ]
validation <- data4[-inTrain, ]

# Initialize H2O
# h2o.init(nthreads = -1)
h2o.init()
train_set <- as.h2o(training, destination_frame = "Training_set")
validation_set <- as.h2o(validation, destination_frame = "Validation_set")
y <- 'Class'
predictor <- setdiff(names(training), y)

# Convert target variable to factor
train_set[, y] <- as.factor(train_set[, y])
validation_set[, y] <- as.factor(validation_set[, y])

# Train models using H2O AutoML
model_h2o <- h2o.automl(x = predictor, y = y, training_frame = train_set, max_models = model_number, seed = 1234, include_algos = algo)
```


### Metrics of the training process for the training dataset
In H2O AutoML, classification model effectiveness is measured using several metrics:

- **Mean Squared Error (MSE)** and **Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)**: Measure average squared errors and their square root, indicating model accuracy.
- **Logarithmic Loss (Logloss)**: Evaluates how close predicted probabilities are to actual class labels; lower values are better.
- **Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)** and **Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUCPR)**: Assess the model's ability to distinguish between classes and the trade-off between precision and recall (for binomial models).
- **R-squared (R²)**: Indicates the proportion of variance explained by the model.
- **Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)**: Balances model fit and complexity; lower values indicate better models.

These metrics help select the best model. For those without a statistical background, a confusion matrix offers a simpler way to evaluate classification effectiveness. It visually represents how samples are classified, showing misclassifications between real and predicted classes.

Classification efficacy depends on three main factors:

1. **Data Quality**
2. **Algorithm Used**
3. **Efficiency of MST Markers** in distinguishing contamination types

This section evaluates the classification accuracy for the training dataset samples.

### Metrics of the training process for the validation dataset
As in the previous section, this section shows the classification performance metrics and the confusion matrix for the validation dataset.

In order to evaluate the performance of the multinomial classification model, both micro-average and macro-average ROC curves are computed, along with their corresponding AUC values. The micro-average ROC/AUC is derived by aggregating the contributions of all classes into a single binary classification task. This is achieved by stacking all true positive, false positive, true negative, and false negative outcomes across all classes, and treating these values as a large binary classification. Conversely, the macro-average ROC/AUC is calculated by first computing individual ROC curves for each class using a one-vs-rest approach, where each class is designated as the positive class while the others are designated as the negative class. The results from all classes are then averaged to produce a single summary curve. In order to ensure smoothness and comparability across classes, linear interpolation was applied between the ROC points prior to the implementation of the averaging process.

### Plots associated to automl best model
This section presents graphs explaining the optimal auto machine learning model selected during training. 

SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) plots illustrate the relationship between input features and model predictions. Each feature is assigned an importance score that reflects its contribution to the prediction outcome:

- **Positive SHAP values**: indicate that the feature increases the likelihood of a higher prediction.
- **Negative SHAP values**: suggest that the feature decreases the prediction value

In binary classification, SHAP plots are particularly useful for evaluating the effectiveness of MST (Microbial Source Tracking) markers. Effective markers typically show well-separated clusters of SHAP values (e.g., red and blue points), indicating strong discriminatory power between the two classes. When points are closely clustered, the marker may have limited ability to distinguish between classes.

Unlike binomial classifications, where a single set of SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values is generated per sample, multinomial classifications require a distinct set of SHAP values for each class per sample. This significantly increases both computational demands and processing time.

Due to this complexity, SHAP visualisations in multinomial classification are typically limited to a single class, which the user selects. The analysis is then conducted using the validation dataset, ensuring that the insights are based on unseen data and reflect the model’s generalisation capability.

This approach allows for a focused interpretation of feature importance for the selected class, while maintaining computational efficiency.

SHAP plots are available for tree-based models.

Another method to identify effective MST parameters is the importance plot, which shows the relative importance of each feature in a trained model. This helps identify features that most influence the model's predictions.

Note: Stacked Ensemble models do not include a variable importance plot due to their complexity.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

Note that SHAP plots are available only for binomial classification or regression models trained using H2O tree-based models, including Random Forest, GBM, and XGBoost algorithms. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res

# Multiclass SHAP summary for every class and only for validation
if (length(unique(data4$Class)) > 2) {

  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)

  # For multinomial classification
  classes <- unique(data4$Class)
  class.selection <- sapply(1:length(classes), function(i) paste(classes[i], "= (", i, ")"))

  
  svDialogs::dlg_message('The current classification is of the multinomial type. The subsequent stage of the process is to select the class for the execution of the SHAP analysis.')$res
  
  repeat {
    # Display input dialog box for class selection
    selection <- svDialogs::dlgInput(
      paste(class.selection, collapse = "\n"),
      "Please, select a class:"
    )$res

    num_input <- as.numeric(selection)

    if (!is.na(num_input) && num_input > 0 && num_input <= length(classes)) {
      break
    } else {
      svDialogs::dlg_message('Please enter a valid response.')$res
    }
  }

  fav_class <- classes[num_input]
  classes <- setdiff(data4$Class, fav_class)

  models <- list()
  shap_values_all <- list()
  test_df_all <- list()

  for (cls in classes) {
    bin_data <- data4 %>% filter(Class %in% c(fav_class, cls))
    bin_data$Class <- factor(bin_data$Class, levels = c(fav_class, cls))

    bin_h2o <- as.h2o(bin_data)
    splits <- h2o.splitFrame(bin_h2o, ratios = 0.7, seed = 1234)
    train_bin <- splits[[1]]
    test_bin <- splits[[2]]

    mdl <- h2o.gbm(
      x = predictor, y = "Class",
      training_frame = train_bin,
      validation_frame = test_bin,
      distribution = "bernoulli",
      seed = 1234,
      ntrees = 50,
      max_depth = 5
    )

    shap <- h2o.predict_contributions(mdl, test_bin)
    shap_df <- as.data.frame(shap)
    shap_df$ID <- 1:nrow(shap_df)

    models[[cls]] <- mdl
    shap_values_all[[cls]] <- shap_df
    test_df_all[[cls]] <- as.data.frame(test_bin)
  }

  for (cls in names(shap_values_all)) {
    shap_df <- shap_values_all[[cls]]
    test_df <- test_df_all[[cls]]
    predictors <- setdiff(names(test_df), "Class")

    shap_long <- shap_df %>%
      pivot_longer(-ID, names_to = "Feature", values_to = "SHAP") %>%
      filter(Feature != "BiasTerm") %>%
      left_join(
        test_df %>%
          mutate(ID = 1:nrow(.)) %>%
          pivot_longer(-c(ID, Class), names_to = "Feature", values_to = "value"),
        by = c("ID", "Feature")
      ) %>%
      group_by(Feature) %>%
      mutate(norm_value = (value - min(value, na.rm = TRUE)) / 
                         (max(value, na.rm = TRUE) - min(value, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
      ungroup()

    top_features <- shap_long %>%
      group_by(Feature) %>%
      summarise(mean_abs = mean(abs(SHAP)), .groups = "drop") %>%
      arrange(desc(mean_abs)) %>%
      slice_head(n =  length(names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[3, ])]))) %>%
      pull(Feature)

    shap_top <- filter(shap_long, Feature %in% top_features)
    shap_top$Feature <- factor(shap_top$Feature, levels = rev(top_features))

    class_labels <- unique(test_df$Class)
    plot_title <- paste0(class_labels[1], " vs ", class_labels[2])
    name.jpeg<-paste(class_labels[1],"_",class_labels[2],'_full_set_SHAP.jpeg',sep='')
   
ggplot(shap_top, aes(x = SHAP, y = Feature, color = Class)) +
geom_point(aes(size = norm_value), alpha = 0.6) +
geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
labs(title = plot_title,x = "SHAP Contribution",y = "Feature",color = "Class",      size = "Normalized\nValue") + scale_color_manual(values = c("#1f78b4", "#e31a1c")) +         theme_minimal(base_size = 14)->plot.shap.full
jpeg(name.jpeg,res = 600, width = 8, height = 10, units = 'in')
print(plot.shap.full)
dev.off()
  }
}
```

## The model is stored in a file.
This section provides the code to save the trained model. This is important because H2O allows uploading a previously trained model to classify new samples without repeating the training process. Ichnaea-MST includes a module to load a trained model, extract information, and classify a new dataset. For more help, refer to the module's help section.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Display a message dialog box 
svDialogs::dlg_message('In the next stage, the trained machine learning model will be saved. This model can be used later with the "UPLOAD MODEL & CLASSIFICATION MODULE" for new classifications. It is recommended to consult the help section of that module for guidance on saving the trained model. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res

repeat {
  # Prompt the user to indicate whether they wish to save the machine learning model in a file
  doyouwant <- svDialogs::dlgInput('Please indicate whether you wish to save the machine learning model in a file (y/n).', password = TRUE)$res
```

## Theoretical model optimisation
H2O Infogram is a graphical tool designed to identify the most valuable and unique features driving the response in supervised classification problems. It plots variables on a two-dimensional grid of total versus net information:
- **X-axis**: Predictive power
- **Y-axis**: Uniqueness of each variable

The infogram generates a graph with a reduced set of MST markers, helping users enhance model efficiency by reducing the number of necessary MST markers.

The script uses three distinct datasets:
- **Training**: 60% of the samples, used to calibrate the model's parameters.
- **Validation**: 20% of the samples, used to evaluate the model's performance, fine-tune hyperparameters, and prevent overfitting.
- **Testing**: 20% of the samples, reserved for final evaluation (performance metrics, confusion matrix, and associated plots).

In this section, users can select the option to reduce MST markers, emphasizing which class needs better identification.

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Dialogbox
svDialogs::dlg_message('The H2O-infogram is a graphical tool for information-theoretic interpretability, helping users quickly identify the key variables that significantly impact the response. It highlights crucial MST markers for classification, allowing for a reduction in predictors, though this may slightly affect classification performance metrics. Since training samples are generated using Monte Carlo methods, the selection of MST markers for the reduced model may vary between simulations. By default, GBM is used as the learning algorithm to construct the infogram. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res 

# Prompt the user to indicate whether they wish to save the machine learning model in a file
  doyouwant.reduction <- svDialogs::dlgInput('Please indicate whether you wish to start the H2O-infogram analysis (y/n).', password = TRUE)$res
 
repeat { 
  # Check if the user input is valid (either 'y', 'Y', 'n', or 'N')
  if (doyouwant.reduction %in% c('y', 'Y', 'n', 'N')) {
    break
  } else {
    # Prompt the user to enter a valid response if the input is invalid
    svDialogs::dlg_message('Please enter a valid response. To continue, please press the "Enter" key or click the "OK" button.')$res
  }
}

# If the user wants to save the machine learning model
if (tolower(doyouwant.reduction) == 'y') {

# Selection of variables
data3[names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[3, ])])] -> data4
data4$Class <- data3$Class

# Split the data into training, validation, and test sets

  data = as.h2o(data4), 
  ratios = c(0.6, 0.2), 
  destination_frames = c("Training_Infogram", "Validation_Infogram", "Testing_Infogram"), seed = 1234)
train <- splits[[1]]
valid <- splits[[2]]
test  <- splits[[3]]
y <- 'Class'
predictor <- setdiff(names(training), y)

# Convert the target variable to a factor
train[, y] <- as.factor(train[, y])
valid[, y] <- as.factor(valid[, y])
test[, y] <- as.factor(test[, y])

# Generate the infogram for the predictors
h2o.infogram(x = predictor, y = y, training_frame = train, validation_frame = valid, nfolds = 10, top_n_features = length(names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[3, ])]))) -> infogram.results
print(plot(infogram.results))

# Save the infogram plot as a JPEG file

dev.off()

You need to specify which response categories are considered "positive/favorable outcomes". If there is a class for "human contamination", please select it. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res

unique(data4$Class) -> classes

repeat {
  # Display input dialog box for the number of models
  selection <- svDialogs::dlgInput(paste(class.selection, collapse = "\n"), "Please input here the number of the class")$res->doyouwant
  num_input <- as.numeric(doyouwant)
  
  # Check if the input is a valid number

    break
  } else {

  }
}

doyouwant<-classes[as.numeric(doyouwant)]
favorable_class.shap<-doyouwant
# Train subset models based on the infogram results
infogram_models <- h2o.infogram_train_subset_models(infogram.results, h2o.gbm, train, valid, y, favorable_class = doyouwant)

# Get the best model from the infogram models
h2o.getModel(infogram_models$model_id[1]) 
infogram.results@admissible_score

# Capture the admissible score details
model_details <- capture.output(print(infogram.results@admissible_score)) 

# Create HTML content for the infogram results
html_content <- tags$html(tags$head(tags$title('Reduced set of MST-predictors')), tags$body(tags$h1("Infogram results"), tags$pre(paste(model_details, collapse = "\n"))))

# Save HTML content to a file
save_html(html_content, file = "Infogram_results.html")

# Select the admissible features from the data
data3[infogram.results@admissible_features] -> data4
data4$Class <- data3$Class

# Split the data into training, validation, and test sets again
splits <- h2o.splitFrame(
  data = as.h2o(data4), 
  ratios = c(0.6, 0.2), 
  destination_frames = c("Training_reduced", "Validation_reduced", "Testing_reduced"), seed = 1234)

train <- splits[[1]]
valid <- splits[[2]]
test  <- splits[[3]]
y <- 'Class'
predictor <- setdiff(names(train), y)

# Convert the target variable to a factor again
train[, y] <- as.factor(train[, y])
valid[, y] <- as.factor(valid[, y])
test[, y] <- as.factor(test[, y])

# Train a GBM model with the reduced set of predictors
h2o.gbm(x = predictor, y = y, training_frame = train, validation_frame = valid, ntrees = 50, max_depth = 0, nfolds = 10) -> model.reduced


# Display a message dialog box 
svDialogs::dlg_message('Next, the learning curve of the model, the significance of the MST markers, and the SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) plots from the H2O-infogram analysis will be saved as a JPEG file. To proceed, press "Enter" or click "OK".')$res

# Plot and save the learning curve for the reduced model
try(h2o.learning_curve_plot(model.reduced))
jpeg('Reduced_set_Learning curve.jpeg', res = 600, width = 5, height = 5, units = 'in')
print(try(h2o.learning_curve_plot(model.reduced)))
dev.off()

# Plot and save the variable importance for the reduced model
print(try(h2o.varimp_plot(model.reduced)))

jpeg('Reduced_set_Importance.jpeg', res = 600, width = 5, height = 5, units = 'in')
print(try(h2o.varimp_plot(model.reduced)))
dev.off()

# Save the SHAP summary plot for the training set as a JPEG file
# Only for binomial (two classes) classification
if (length(unique(data4$Class))==2){
print(try(h2o.shap_summary_plot(model.reduced, test)))
jpeg('Reduced_set_SHAP.jpeg', res = 600, width = 5, height = 5, units = 'in')
print(try(h2o.shap_summary_plot(model.reduced, test)))
dev.off()
} else {
  
 fav_class <- favorable_class.shap
  classes <- setdiff(classes, favorable_class.shap)

  models <- list()
  shap_values_all <- list()
  test_df_all <- list()

  for (cls in classes) {
    bin_data <- data4 %>% filter(Class %in% c(fav_class, cls))
    bin_data$Class <- factor(bin_data$Class, levels = c(fav_class, cls))

    bin_h2o <- as.h2o(bin_data)
    splits <- h2o.splitFrame(bin_h2o, ratios = 0.7, seed = 1234)
    train_bin <- splits[[1]]
    test_bin <- splits[[2]]

    mdl <- h2o.gbm(
      x = predictor, y = "Class",
      training_frame = train_bin,
      validation_frame = test_bin,
      distribution = "bernoulli",
      seed = 1234,
      ntrees = 50,
      max_depth = 5
    )

    shap <- h2o.predict_contributions(mdl, test_bin)
    shap_df <- as.data.frame(shap)
    shap_df$ID <- 1:nrow(shap_df)

    models[[cls]] <- mdl
    shap_values_all[[cls]] <- shap_df
    test_df_all[[cls]] <- as.data.frame(test_bin)
  }

  for (cls in names(shap_values_all)) {
    shap_df <- shap_values_all[[cls]]
    test_df <- test_df_all[[cls]]
    predictors <- setdiff(names(test_df), "Class")

    shap_long <- shap_df %>%
      pivot_longer(-ID, names_to = "Feature", values_to = "SHAP") %>%
      filter(Feature != "BiasTerm") %>%
      left_join(
        test_df %>%
          mutate(ID = 1:nrow(.)) %>%
          pivot_longer(-c(ID, Class), names_to = "Feature", values_to = "value"),
        by = c("ID", "Feature")
      ) %>%
      group_by(Feature) %>%
      mutate(norm_value = (value - min(value, na.rm = TRUE)) / 
                         (max(value, na.rm = TRUE) - min(value, na.rm = TRUE))) %>%
      ungroup()

    top_features <- shap_long %>%
      group_by(Feature) %>%
      summarise(mean_abs = mean(abs(SHAP)), .groups = "drop") %>%
      arrange(desc(mean_abs)) %>%
      slice_head(n =  length(names(metadata[, grep(1, metadata[3, ])]))) %>%
      pull(Feature)

    shap_top <- filter(shap_long, Feature %in% top_features)
    shap_top$Feature <- factor(shap_top$Feature, levels = rev(top_features))

    class_labels <- unique(test_df$Class)
    plot_title <- paste0(class_labels[1], " vs ", class_labels[2])
    name.jpeg<-paste(class_labels[1],"_",class_labels[2],'_reduced_set_SHAP.jpeg',sep='')
   
ggplot(shap_top, aes(x = SHAP, y = Feature, color = Class)) +
geom_point(aes(size = norm_value), alpha = 0.6) +
geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
labs(title = plot_title,x = "SHAP Contribution",y = "Feature",color = "Class",      size = "Normalized\nValue") + scale_color_manual(values = c("#1f78b4", "#e31a1c")) +         theme_minimal(base_size = 14)->plot.shap.full
jpeg(name.jpeg,res = 600, width = 8, height = 10, units = 'in')
print(plot.shap.full)
dev.off() 
  }
}

# Generate and print the confusion matrix for the reduced model
print(try(h2o.confusionMatrix(model.reduced, test)))

  
# Displays the samples which are under the LOD
```

```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# AUC Metrics with interpolated average ROC (macro) for multinomial distribution

# Load required libraries
library(multiROC)
library(ggplot2)

# Predict probabilities from H2O model
predictions <- h2o.predict(model.reduced, test)

#  Extract true labels and predicted probabilities
y_true <- as.vector(test[,'Class'])
y_probs <- as.data.frame(predictions)[, -1]  # remove predicted class column

class_names <- colnames(y_probs)

#  One-hot encode true labels manually
y_true <- factor(y_true, levels = class_names)  # ensure same order
true_df <- as.data.frame(sapply(class_names, function(class) as.integer(y_true == class)))
colnames(true_df) <- paste0(class_names, "_true")

#  Rename predicted probabilities
colnames(y_probs) <- paste0(class_names, "_pred_m1")

#  Combine into one data frame for multiROC
multi_df <- cbind(true_df, y_probs)

#  Compute ROC curves
roc_res <- multi_roc(multi_df, force_diag = TRUE)

# Prepare data for ggplot
plot_df <- plot_roc_data(roc_res)


# Extract and print AUC values directly and build a clean data frame
annotation_df <- data.frame(
  Group = c(class_names, "Macro", "Micro"),
  AUC = as.numeric(unlist(roc_res$AUC))
)

cat('\n','AUC-Values of the multinomial classification','\n')
print(annotation_df)

# Plot using ggplot2 with facets
print(ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = 1 - Specificity, y = Sensitivity)) +
  geom_path(aes(color = Group), size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Group, scales = "fixed") +
  labs(title = "Multiclass ROC Curves (multiROC)",x = "1-Specifity",y = "Sensitivity"  ) + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = 'bold'), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 16), axis.title.y = element_text(size = 16), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14, angle = 90), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 14), legend.text = element_text(size = 14), legend.title = element_text(size = 16, face = 'bold'), strip.text = element_text(size = 16,face = 'bold'), legend.position = "bottom")  + geom_text(data = annotation_df, aes(x = 0.6, y = 0.2, label = sprintf("AUC = %.8f", AUC)), size = 5, color = "black"))

# Save the plot
jpeg('ROC curves multinomial reduced model.jpeg', res = 600, width = 10, height = 10, units = 'in')
print(ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = 1 - Specificity, y = Sensitivity)) +
  geom_path(aes(color = Group), size = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Group, scales = "fixed") +
  labs(title = "Multiclass ROC Curves (multiROC)",x = "1-Specifity",y = "Sensitivity"  ) + theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = 'bold'), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 16), axis.title.y = element_text(size = 16), axis.text.x = element_text(size = 14, angle = 90), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 14), legend.text = element_text(size = 14), legend.title = element_text(size = 16, face = 'bold'), strip.text = element_text(size = 16,face = 'bold'), legend.position = "bottom")  + geom_text(data = annotation_df, aes(x = 0.6, y = 0.2, label = sprintf("AUC = %.8f", AUC)), size = 5, color = "black"))
dev.off()
```

# Classification
This section initiates the classification process. Two key points to emphasize:

1. **Dataset Structure**: The dataset must have the correct structure for classification. Refer to the help documentation for details.
2. **H2O Framework**: There's no need to remove extra variables not found in the trained models (including the reduced model), so the user doesn't need to modify the original data structure.

## Print and save in a file the result of the classification of the samples with all the predictors
